answer.exemplar: The right-hand rule gives v cross B, which is the force direction only for a positive charge. The electron carries negative charge, so the true force is q times v cross B with q negative, which flips the direction by 180 degrees. Finger along v, curl toward B, and the thumb gives the positive-charge force; reverse it for the electron.

questions.explanation: v cross B gives the force direction for a positive charge. A negative charge multiplies by a negative q, reversing the direction. The rule was applied correctly; the sign of the charge was left out, so the answer was flipped.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a charged particle keeps a constant speed in a uniform field
questions.stem: A charged particle in a uniform field draws a perfect circle. Explain why the speed stays constant even though a force is clearly acting.

answer.exemplar: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it can only bend the path, never add or remove kinetic energy. With the speed fixed, the centripetal force mv squared over r stays constant and the radius r = mv/(qB) is fixed, so the particle traces a circle whose centre lies on the line of the field. questions.explanation: The magnetic force does no work because it stays perpendicular to the velocity, so kinetic energy and speed are constant. The force then acts as the centripetal force, giving a fixed radius and a circular path.

Cross your fingers along v and curl toward B, and the thumb gives v cross B for a positive charge, reversed for a negative one. Doing the algebra removes the guesswork that flipping the geometry by hand causes.

questions.explanation: A fixed procedure beats mental rotation: write components, expand the cross product by determinant, then check with the hand rule. Hand rules alone cause three-dimensional errors, and they apply to v cross B as a whole.
